# containerd Drop-in Configuration and NVIDIA GPUs

KubeSolo runs its own embedded containerd and generates that containerd's configuration on every start. To add runtimes or change containerd settings, write a drop-in file. KubeSolo loads drop-ins on top of its generated configuration.

This page covers how drop-ins work and walks through the most common use: running NVIDIA GPU workloads.

---

## How It Works

On every start, KubeSolo writes the containerd configuration to:

```
/var/lib/kubesolo/containerd/config.toml
```

**Do not edit this file.** KubeSolo overwrites it on every start, so any changes you make there are lost on the next restart.

The generated configuration imports every `*.toml` file from these directories:

| Directory | Notes |
|---|---|
| `/etc/containerd/conf.d/` | The standard drop-in directory. `nvidia-ctk` and containerd packaging use it too. Use this one. |
| `/etc/containerd/config.d/` | Still loaded, so drop-ins written for KubeSolo 1.2.1 and earlier keep working. |

containerd merges the drop-ins into the generated configuration in file-name order, so a numeric prefix such as `99-` controls which file wins. Neither directory has to exist.

containerd reads drop-ins only at startup. After you add or change one, restart KubeSolo:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart kubesolo
```

> **Note:** KubeSolo 1.2.1 and earlier only loaded `/etc/containerd/config.d/`. If you're on one of those releases, put your drop-ins there.

### Drop-in format

The generated configuration uses containerd config **version 3**, so drop-ins must use version 3 plugin names as well. For example, use `io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime`, not the version 2 name `io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri`:

```toml
version = 3

[plugins."io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime".containerd.runtimes.<name>]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2"
```

containerd ignores tables that use version 2 names, and it doesn't report an error when it does.

---

## NVIDIA GPUs

This setup uses the NVIDIA driver and NVIDIA Container Toolkit that are already installed on the host. It adds an `nvidia` runtime to KubeSolo's containerd and then installs the NVIDIA device plugin (or the GPU Operator) with its driver and toolkit installation turned off.

### 1. Check the host

```bash
nvidia-smi
nvidia-ctk --version
command -v nvidia-container-runtime
nvidia-ctk cdi list
```

If any of these fail, install the NVIDIA driver and the [NVIDIA Container Toolkit](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/container-toolkit/latest/install-guide.html) on the host before continuing.

### 2. Add the `nvidia` runtime

Create `/etc/containerd/conf.d/99-nvidia.toml`:

```toml
version = 3

[plugins."io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime".containerd.runtimes.nvidia]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2"
  snapshotter = "overlayfs"

[plugins."io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime".containerd.runtimes.nvidia.options]
  BinaryName = "/usr/bin/nvidia-container-runtime"
  SystemdCgroup = true
```

- Set `BinaryName` to the path that `command -v nvidia-container-runtime` printed. On some distributions it is `/usr/sbin/nvidia-container-runtime`.
- `SystemdCgroup` must match the cgroup driver KubeSolo uses. KubeSolo uses `true` on hosts that run systemd with cgroup v2, and `false` everywhere else, for example OpenRC hosts or cgroup v1.

Then restart KubeSolo and confirm containerd loaded the runtime:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart kubesolo
sudo crictl --runtime-endpoint unix:///var/lib/kubesolo/containerd/containerd.sock info \
  | grep -A3 '"nvidia"'
```

> **Using `nvidia-ctk runtime configure`?** It writes its drop-in to `/etc/containerd/conf.d/99-nvidia.toml` by default, which KubeSolo now loads. Check that the generated file uses `version = 3` and the `io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime` plugin name described above.

### 3. Create the RuntimeClass

```yaml
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: nvidia
handler: nvidia
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f nvidia-runtimeclass.yaml
```

`handler` must match the runtime name used in the drop-in (`runtimes.nvidia`).

### 4. Install the device plugin or the GPU Operator

Install one of these two. Neither needs to install the driver or toolkit because they are already on the host.

**NVIDIA device plugin:**

```bash
helm repo add nvdp https://nvidia.github.io/k8s-device-plugin
helm upgrade -i nvdp nvdp/nvidia-device-plugin \
  --namespace nvidia-device-plugin --create-namespace \
  --version 0.20.1 \
  --set runtimeClassName=nvidia \
  --set gfd.enabled=true \
  --set nfd.enabled=false
```

**GPU Operator:**

```bash
helm repo add nvidia https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia
helm install --wait --generate-name \
  -n gpu-operator --create-namespace \
  nvidia/gpu-operator --version=v26.7.1 \
  --set driver.enabled=false \
  --set toolkit.enabled=false \
  --set nfd.enabled=false
```

Keep `toolkit.enabled=false`. The operator's toolkit container would otherwise edit `/var/lib/kubesolo/containerd/config.toml`, which KubeSolo overwrites on the next start. Use the drop-in from step 2 instead.

### 5. Run a test workload

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: cuda-smoke
spec:
  runtimeClassName: nvidia
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: cuda
      image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-base-ubuntu24.04
      command: ["nvidia-smi"]
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 1
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f cuda-smoke.yaml
kubectl logs -f cuda-smoke
```

If everything is set up correctly, the pod's logs show the same `nvidia-smi` table you saw on the host.

---

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| Pod fails with `no runtime for "nvidia" is configured` | containerd didn't load the drop-in. Check the directory (`conf.d`, or `config.d` on 1.2.1 and earlier), check that the file ends in `.toml`, and restart KubeSolo. |
| Runtime is missing from `crictl info` even though the file is in the right place | The drop-in uses version 2 plugin names. Rewrite it with `version = 3` and `io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime`. |
| Edits to `/var/lib/kubesolo/containerd/config.toml` disappear | KubeSolo regenerates that file on every start. Use a drop-in instead. |
| Pod is stuck in `Pending` with `Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu` | The device plugin isn't running, or it was installed without `runtimeClassName=nvidia`. |
